question: v10
q: How's the job market looking for women in Victoria?

transcript.answer:
The job market for women in Victoria has got noticeably weaker over the past year. The worst seems to have stopped in the last couple of months, but it hasn't really recovered.

**Latest figures (September 2026, seasonally adjusted, Victorian women)**

| Measure | Sep 2026 | Sep 2025 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unemployment rate | **5.1%** | 4.1% | +1.0 pts |
| Participation rate | 63.6% | 63.9% | −0.3 pts |
| Employment-to-population | 60.4% | 61.3% | −0.9 pts |
| Employed | 1,843,000 | 1,838,000 | +5,000 (+0.3%) |
| – Full-time | 1,008,000 | 1,011,000 | about flat |
| – Part-time* | about 835,000 | about 828,000 | +7,000 |

*Part-time is total employed minus full-time.

**What's happened**
- **Unemployment has risen.** Women's unemployment stayed around 3.9–4.1% for most of 2025. It started climbing in early 2026, hit 5.1% in June and peaked at 5.2% in July. In August and September it eased only slightly, to about 5.1%.
- **Jobs fell, then came back.** The number of employed women dropped by about 36,000 between December 2025 and April 2026, to 1.80 million. Since then that loss has been almost fully regained. Over the year, though, women's employment has barely grown (+0.3%), while the female population kept growing. That's why a smaller share of women have jobs (60.4%, down from 61.3%).
- **No growth in full-time work.** Full-time jobs for women are slightly down on a year ago. The small increase in jobs has all been part-time.
- **Participation is holding up.** At 63.6%, it's close to last year's level, after dipping to 62.4% in April. Women haven't left the workforce in large numbers. Because more are looking for work but not finding it, unemployment has gone up.

**Compared with men in Victoria (September 2026)**
Men's unemployment rate is about the same, at 5.0%. So the weakness is across Victoria's whole job market rather than specific to women. Men's participation is much higher (71.5%) but has fallen over the past few months, from 72.1% in June.

**Caveat:** State figures split by sex come from a fairly small survey sample, so they can jump around from month to month. It's better to look at the trend over several months than at any single month. Even so, the move from about 4% to about 5% unemployment has lasted since mid-2026, so it looks like a real shift.
